lectures.title: Outro: Best Practices and Common Challenges

cues.en: Let's now have an outro here to this chapter because I still want to say a few words.
One thing that I would like to tell you is that you can give yourself an optional exercise.
You could delete an important file that it needed that is needed during boot and then try to restore
it with a live DVD or a recovery system.
If you work in a company and you have colleagues, then it would be of course better to ask a colleague,
just delete a file that's important for the boot process.
And then you have a system where you can just debug that.
Another thing is that if you would be the sysadmin of a server for example, and you don't have physical
access to that computer, then you should of course try to do that with a separate server that's running
in the same environment because the recovery system from a server usually looks different.
You have a back end to that server and there you can be like, Hey, I want to boot a recovery system
on that computer and then you need to connect to that one and you only have a bash available there.
So, so in that case, you could also train that.
The reason why this makes sense is, especially if you are expecting that in the future some real serious
problems might happen.
And then you need it's really important that you act fast and that you can quickly identify the problem.
Then it might make sense to practice that 1 or 2 times.
The next thing is, if you're running an actual server and something like this happens for quite a few
servers, it is possible to make a backup even if the system doesn't boot.
That's especially the case for virtual servers where it's not running directly on physical hardware,
but there's an abstraction layer in between.
Then sometimes it's possible to really just create a snapshot.
So if something during the troubleshooting breaks and you completely destroy the system, then at least
the data is still there.
The same is, by the way, also applies when you boot up with to the live system.
If it doesn't take too long, it's always a good idea to just make a full backup, at least from all
the directories that are needed for your company with the data in them before doing the actual troubleshooting.
If you can afford the that it will take a little bit longer, then it's always a judgment call for that.
Um, yeah.
The next thing is when you are running an actual server, problems with the bootloader are a bit more
tedious in the sense that you might not be able to see the bootloader.
So debugging is a little bit more difficult if you can't see and visualize it.
But there are also solutions.
I mean, it depends on your hosting provider, on the provider that you're renting the server from.
But for example, um, I was renting from a uh, company and they offer a server they call the, the
service remote hands.
It's extremely expensive.
They charge by every 15 minutes they charge you more, but they have the possibility to go to the physical
server with an actual monitor and do debugging for you.
So that would actually also be an option that you might want to consider.
I just want to let you know that stuff like this does exist, but of course the company that you work
with, they must, uh, offer that.
The next thing that I would still like to mention is what are common problems?
Problems can be happen during the boot process.
In our case, that was a problem with the kernel, but it could also be a problem with mounts that a
file system doesn't work.
Maybe an SSD is old and the file system can't be read anymore.
Then the gparted, the the partition or F check for example, would talk about or would mention problems
there if you would run that one.
It's also the case that you might have installed a few packages that cause problems.
Usually all packages should work, but.
Maybe from some third party providers or I mean, there might always be some inconsistencies or something
that doesn't work.
So additional packages can always cause problems.
The hardware can break as well.
Um, I have to admit this is a little bit more difficult to find.
So for example, let's say our system is slow because the CPU is hot and because there's dust in the
fan.
Um.
I might not suspect that at first.
I might first suspect.
Okay, maybe there's just too much software running on the computer and this might something that I
might not be aware of.
Um, usually, actually, I think a fan and servers, they're extremely powerful and really, really
fast.
So there should be enough headroom that even if a fan doesn't run the way it's supposed to, it should
still work.
And if it breaks, probably the data center will be notified.
So most likely stuff like this the data center will take care of.
But just be aware that there might also be actual hardware problems involved in in problems.
In our case, we got lucky because it happened during an update or upgrade of our system.
So and I even got an error message with a hint pointing me to the kernel.
So it was pretty clear that it's not a hardware issue, but something related to packages or kernel.
Um, there might also be problems while the system is running.
For example, services might not start or services might crash or there's just high CPU load.
But for all all of those problems we usually still can connect to our um, system.
And then we also have proper log files to identify those problems.
So those problems also happen, but they usually don't involve a live system in order to fix it.
Um, another thing that I also would like to mention would be, for example, that there might be wrongly
configured software.
So for example, the software, if it's a remote server that allows us to connect to that one, or for
example, we might have configured a firewall in an improper way and then we are no longer able to connect
to that computer.
And in that case, the way to go would well, actually for that one, if we had a problem with the firewall,
we might have to use a live system to fix that one to change the configuration file.
So there you can see there might be a lot of different problems happening and it will be your job as
a sysadmin to manage all of those and ensure that everything runs smoothly.
Probably this list is not complete and there are a lot of more cases for problems on Linux systems,
but I hope I could give you a rough overview and I also hope that you will never use the knowledge here
of that chapter.
But if you do need to use it, I hope that it will help you get the system running faster again.
So this would be my advice for troubleshooting and how to rescue a Linux system.
